title: The "BLOOM-AI" Framework Represents Everything We're Getting Wrong About AI and Learning
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick dissects the 'BLOOM-AI Framework', a LinkedIn-circulated scheme for using AI in teaching, as an emblem of how the sector is misframing AI and learning. He first attacks its pyramid version of Bloom's taxonomy, arguing that it demotes factual knowledge and confuses the form of an AI-generated activity with its actual cognitive demand. He then challenges the framework's claim that AI is 'scaffolding', noting that true scaffolding fades while AI tools tend toward permanent dependency and 'cosplaying domain knowledge'. He also condemns its inclusion of learning styles as a debunked myth. In the second half Hendrick sets out what he sees as AI's genuine promise: 'cognitive complementarity' that could orchestrate retrieval, spacing and interleaving at a precision humans have never managed. His conclusion is that AI should reduce cognitive noise rather than cognitive effort, and that frameworks must start from how people learn rather than from pyramids and myths.
points: Hendrick's 'taxonomic fallacy': treating Bloom's taxonomy as a rigid hierarchy lets a framework label AI-generated multiple-choice questions as 'Create' when they may only automate recall.
He argues AI cannot be scaffolding in Bruner, Wood and Ross's sense because scaffolding fades with competence, whereas AI use can harden into dependency.
Drawing on Willingham, he warns that students who outsource ideas and structure to AI build shallow fluency but fragile understanding, since the learning lies in the effort of producing the thing.
His positive case is that AI's data capacity might finally reveal how retrieval, spacing and interleaving interact dynamically, moving the field from 'weather folklore to meteorological modelling'.
The governing principle he offers: AI should reduce cognitive noise, not cognitive effort.
quotes: The pyramid promotes the misconception that “lower-order” components like facts and knowledge are somehow less valuable or that they must be “gotten through” before the real learning happens. In reality, factual knowledge is the substrate from which all higher-order thinking grows. I’ll just say it again: you can’t connect the dots if you don’t have any dots.

More problematically, it conflates the form of an activity with its cognitive demand. Having students use AI to generate multiple-choice questions (mapped to "Create") doesn't necessarily engage higher-order thinking. It may simply automate lower-order recall dressed in creative clothing.

AI tools, however, can tend toward permanent dependency rather than progressive autonomy. Students may become more sophisticated at prompting and curating AI outputs without developing the underlying disciplinary thinking the AI is ostensibly supporting.

The result is a kind of intellectual outsourcing that short-circuits schema construction and leaves students with shallow fluency but fragile understanding. The point is not producing the thing, it’s the effort in producing the thing.
Humans have a bad track record at systemising this if we are being brutally honest. I used to think that retrieval practice would be the simplest thing to get right in a classroom. How wrong I was.

It's moving from the equivalent of weather folklore to meteorological modelling and finally having the computational power to make sense of learning's complex, dynamic systems. The key insight for me is that AI should reduce cognitive noise, not cognitive effort - supporting the conditions under which deep learning flourishes.
In the end, the problem isn’t AI. It’s how we frame it. When we wrap faulty theories in sleek design and powerful tech, we risk scaling confusion rather than clarity.
